newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong stocks close lower, pulled down by HSBC.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong stocks close lower, pulled down by HSBC.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks closed lower on Wednesday, after falling steadily in late afternoon, chiefly on selling in HSBC Holdings and a lack of buying interest before a U.S. Federal Reserve policy meeting, brokers said.

"Next week is a big week and investors don't want to roll the dice in advance of the FOMC meeting," said James Osborn, vice president at ING Barings. "I think we have actually seen a net outflow of funds from Hong Kong recently."

The Hang Seng Index closed 97.49 points lower at 12,651.42, near its low for the day of 12,650.29. Turnover rose to HK$8.12 billion, slightly higher than Tuesday's HK$7.52 billion. The FOMC meeting will set the tone for the market in coming months, said Osborn. The U.S. central bank's Federal Open Market Committee will meet to set lending rates on March 25.

The index futures market appeared to lead the market higher in late morning and early afternoon, but the trend was not strong enough. The March contract closed 15 points lower at 12,670, a fair premium with the cash market.
"Futures should be quiet in advance of the FOMC meeting, and could be very volatile on Wednesday, said Steven Chu in Sassoon Futures.
The property sector led the market down, followed by banks.
"The property investment companies looked terrible today," said a broker with a Singaporean house.
Great Eagle dropped HK$1.80 to HK$26.25 on low turnover of HK$41.53 million.
Market talk said Wharf's results due out on Friday would be disappointing, pointing to low rental reversions and slower earnings growth for the entire sector, brokers said.
Property-based conglomerate Wharf slid HK$1.05 to HK$29.25. Henderson Land which is to report its first-half 1997 earnings later on Wednesday, added HK$0.25 to HK$64.75.
Weakness in banking giant HSBC Holdings pulled the index down in mid-afternoon. The share lost HK$2.00 to HK$180.50 on turnover of HK$415.52 million.
"They are selling the relative outperformance of the bank," said Angus Shillington, institutional sales manager at Asia Equity. "We could see it fall further."

Pearl Oriental was the second most actively traded issue. The share rose HK$0.10 to HK$6.45. Investors were pleased with the company's 74.1 percent rise in 1996 net profit, announced on Tuesday, and its diversification into the hotel industry, the Singaporean broker said.
